title: Linked List Pointers: Merge Two Sorted Lists
oneLiner: Splice the existing nodes into one sorted list: a dummy head, a tail pointer, and at each step attach whichever list's front node is smaller.
keyTakeaway: Merging linked lists needs no new nodes and no extra array: you only change Next pointers. Start from a dummy node, keep a tail pointer to the last node attached, and when one list runs out, attach the whole rest of the other in a single assignment.
explanation:
Given the heads of two singly linked lists, each sorted in ascending order, return one sorted list made of all their nodes. 1 -> 2 -> 4 and 1 -> 3 -> 4 merge into 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 4. The comparison logic is the same as merging two sorted arrays; what changes is that you don't write into an output buffer. You relink the nodes that already exist, so the extra space is O(1).

Create a dummy node and a tail pointer that starts on it. While both lists still have nodes, look at the two front nodes, a and b. Attach the smaller one with tail.Next = smaller, advance that list's pointer past it, and move tail = tail.Next. On a tie take from the first list, which keeps the merge stable (equal values keep their original order). When one list is empty, the other is already sorted and every value in it is at least as big as everything attached so far, so tail.Next = the rest of it finishes the job in one step. Return dummy.Next.

The dummy node removes the awkward first step: without it you'd have to decide which list provides the head before the loop, and handle either list being empty separately. With it, the first attachment works exactly like every other one.

This splice is a building block. Merge sort on a linked list splits the list at the middle (fast and slow pointers) and merges the halves with this function, sorting in a guaranteed, stable O(n log n) with no extra array, which is why it is the usual choice for lists. Merging k lists can pair them up and merge repeatedly, or use a heap.

The visualization shows the merged chain growing from the dummy; the message shows what's left of each input list.

Return dummy.Next: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 6 -> 7 -> 9 -> null. No new nodes were created.

recognitionSignals: Two (or a few) inputs are each already sorted linked lists and the output is one sorted list.
The result should reuse the input nodes, or O(1) extra space is required.
A linked list merge sort, or any step that combines two sorted runs of nodes.
gotchas: Forgetting to advance tail after attaching a node means every attachment overwrites the previous one.
After the loop, attach the leftover list with one assignment. Looping over it node by node works but misses the point, and forgetting it entirely drops the largest values.
Return dummy.Next, not dummy: the dummy's own value is not part of the answer.
confusableWith: Sorting: Merge Two Sorted Arrays (Fundamentals) uses the same compare-the-fronts loop but copies values into a new array. With linked lists you relink existing nodes instead, and the leftover tail is attached in O(1) rather than copied.
K-way Merge: Merge K Sorted Arrays (this track) merges many sorted inputs with a min-heap of the k current fronts. With only two inputs, one comparison per step does the job and a heap adds nothing.

complexity.note: Each step attaches one node from one of the lists, and the leftover tail is attached in one assignment, so at most n + m steps. Existing nodes are relinked, so the only extra memory is the dummy node and the tail pointer.

referenceSolutions.python:
def merge_two_lists(a, b):
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    tail = dummy
    while a is not None and b is not None:
        if a.val <= b.val:  # ties take from a, which keeps the merge stable
            tail.next = a
            a = a.next
        else:
            tail.next = b
            b = b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a if a is not None else b  # the leftover list is already sorted
    return dummy.next
